Pulmonary Dyspnea

Forced Expiration 
The simplest test of lung function.
It needs minimal equipment → highly informative. 
Patients with lung disease have an abnormal forced expiration volume. 
Used to evaluate chronic dyspnea. 
Valuable in detecting asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases.

Forced Expiration 
The forced expiratory volume (FEV1) is the volume of gas exhaled in 1 second by a forced expiration from full inspiration. The vital capacity is the total volume of gas that can be exhaled after a full inspiration.

Note: It is important when recording normal respiration that the volunteer is facing away from the computer screen and is not consciously controlling breathing. 
Exercise 1: Practice how to use the spirometer

Exercise 2: Lung volumes and capacities
Objectives
In this exercise, the respiratory cycle and changes in flow and volume will be examined.
Procedure
Note: It is important when recording normal respiration that the volunteer is facing away from the computer screen and is not consciously controlling breathing. 
The flow head must be left undisturbed on the bench during the zeroing process. Choose the Spirometer Pod… from the Flow channel Function pop-up menu. Click the Zero button to re-zero the Spirometer Pod. When zeroing has finished, click the OK button to return to the Chart View.
Ask the volunteer to breathe normally through the flow head. Record normal tidal breathing for 20 seconds. Add the comment “Normal tidal breathing” to the Chart trace.
Click Stop to end the recording. Click Start to restart the recording.
At the end of a normal tidal inspiration ask the volunteer to breathe in as deeply as possible and then to breathe normally. 
At the end of a normal tidal expiration ask the volunteer to exhale as deeply as possible and then to breathe normally.

Exercise 3: Pulmonary function tests
Objectives
In this exercise, parameters of forced expiration used in evaluating pulmonary function are measured. 
Procedure
Re-zero the flow head using steps 1-2 from the procedures in Exercise 2.
Click the Start button to begin recording.  
Have the volunteer breathe normally for 30 seconds.
Ask the volunteer to inhale maximally and then exhale as forcefully and fully as possible (i.e., inhale maximally and exhale until no more air can be expired). Press Enter to add the comment. After a few seconds, the volunteer should let their breathing return to normal.
Click Stop to end recording.
Repeat steps 2–6 twice more, so that there are three separate forced breath recordings.

Case study for lab
Ralph, a 43-year-old male has a history of asthma since childhood. His asthma triggers are pollen and cold weather, causing wheezing and shortness of breath. He used a bronchodilator (albuterol, a β2-adrenergic agonist) to treat attacks. At the time of his death, his asthma attacks were severe and frequent, with him visiting the ER five times in the past year. 
Three days before he died, Ralph had an upper respiratory infection, with nasal and chest congestion and a fever of 39 °C. He was exhausted from “just trying to breathe,” and the bronchodilator was ineffective. 
On admission, auscultation revealed inspiratory and expiratory wheezes, with severe respiratory distress.
